detail: supported
The spatial skeleton is a complete octree that recursively subdivides the volume spatially until all subvolumes reach a predefined minimum size [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the spatial skeleton is a complete octree that recursively subdivides the volume spatially until all subvolumes reach a predefined minimum size. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.1, stating: 'The skeleton of a TSP tree is equivalent to a regular complete octree, which recursively subdivides the volume spatially until all subvolumes reach a predefined minimum size.' Additionally, the notes mention that leaf nodes are volume bricks with a predefined minimum size, and subdivision stops when this size is reached. Therefore, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.
supported
The user-supplied error tolerance for temporal coherence ($\epsilon_{temp}$) identifies regions where rendered images can be reused across several time steps [S1, unofficial].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S1]. Specifically, the notes section states: 'User-supplied error tolerance for temporal coherence, used to identify regions where rendered images can be reused across several time steps.' Additionally, the passage from section 3.2 confirms this: 'The error tolerance for the temporal coherence... is used to identify regions where their volume rendered images can be reused across several time steps.'
supported
Each octree node contains a binary time tree representing the time span $[0, t]$ [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 3.1 that 'each TSP tree node itself is a binary tree in the time span [0, t] associated with the time-varying field.' This directly supports the claim that each octree node contains a binary time tree representing the time span [0, t].
supported
Let $v_{i,t}$ be the value of voxel $i$ at time step $t$, and $A$ be the total number of voxels in the subvolume across all time steps [S1, unofficial].

The claim defines $v_{i,t}$ as the value of voxel $i$ at time step $t$ and $A$ as the total number of voxels in the subvolume across all time steps. Source [S1] explicitly states in the section describing the TSP tree data structure: 'where v_{i,t} is the value of voxel i at time step t, and A is the total number of voxels in the subvolume across all the time steps.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
Render gathered subvolumes independently using a divide-and-conquer paradigm; the final image is a composition of intermediate results [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method renders gathered subvolumes independently using a divide-and-conquer paradigm and that the final image is a composition of intermediate results. Source [S1] explicitly contains the sentence: 'Render gathered subvolumes independently using a divide-and-conquer paradigm; final image is a composition of intermediate results.' Additionally, the source describes the process of recursively traversing the tree (divide-and-conquer) and saving intermediate rendering results in TSP tree nodes, which are then composed.
supported
It should be used for out-of-core rendering of large-scale time-varying volumes where temporal coherence is present [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the proposed algorithm and data structure (TSP tree) are designed to address challenges in 'out-of-core applications' by minimizing I/O overhead. It further notes that 'temporal coherence is frequently present in a time-series volume' and that the algorithm exploits this coherence to accelerate rendering. Therefore, the claim that it should be used for out-of-core rendering of large-scale time-varying volumes where temporal coherence is present is fully supported by the text.
supported
Every node in the binary time tree represents the same spatial subdomain but a different time span [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that every node in the binary time tree represents the same spatial subdomain but a different time span. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 3.1: 'Every node in the binary time tree of a TSP tree node represents the same subdomain in the volume but a different time span.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
If nodes with high temporal coherence are encountered and stored intermediate results cover the current time step, skip rendering and reuse results [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that if nodes with high temporal coherence are encountered and stored intermediate results cover the current time step, rendering is skipped and results are reused. Source [S1] explicitly states in its notes: 'When rendering a different time step, repeat traversal. If nodes with high temporal coherence are encountered and stored intermediate results cover the current time step, skip rendering and reuse results.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported

Strengths include decoupling spatial and temporal domains to effectively detect temporal coherence even when spatial variation is high, reducing I/O overhead for out-of-core applications, allowing runtime trade-offs between image quality and rendering speed via user-supplied tolerances, and maintaining visibility order and spatial locality during traversal [S1, unofficial].

The claim lists four specific strengths of the TSP tree method described in Source [S1]. 1) 'Decoupling spatial and temporal domains...': The evidence explicitly states the TSP tree 'decouples spatial and temporal domains' to avoid issues where 'high spatial variation masks temporal coherence'. 2) 'Reducing I/O overhead for out-of-core applications': The evidence states the algorithm 'minimizes' I/O overhead and is 'suitable for out-of-core applications'. 3) 'Allowing runtime trade-offs... via user-supplied tolerances': The evidence confirms the algorithm 'allows the user to supply the desired error tolerances at run time for the purpose of image-quality/rendering-speed trade-off'. 4) 'Maintaining visibility order and spatial locality during traversal': The evidence states the design intention is to 'maintain the visibility order and spatial locality among the subvolumes in the process of TSP tree traversing'. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
The structure was implemented with an application-controlled demand paging system for out-of-core rendering [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that the system was 'Implemented with an application-controlled demand paging system proposed by Cox and Ellsworth for out-of-core rendering.' This directly confirms every part of the claim.
unsupported
The standard deviation of each voxel over the time span is computed, then these values are averaged [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the standard deviation of each voxel over time is computed, and then these values are averaged. However, the evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines 'Temporal Coherence' as the mean of individual voxels' standard deviations over time. It distinguishes this from the 'Standard Deviation' stored in each node, which is defined as the standard deviation of voxel values in the subvolume across all time steps in that span (a spatial statistic over time, not a temporal statistic per voxel). The claim conflates the definition of the node's standard deviation with the definition of temporal coherence, or misinterprets the calculation method. Specifically, the evidence says: 'To quantify a volume's temporal coherence... we propose to use the mean of the individual voxels’ standard deviations over time.' It does not say the 'standard deviation of each voxel' is the primary value averaged to define the node's standard deviation; rather, the node stores a standard deviation (spatial variance over time) and a separate temporal coherence measure (mean of temporal variances).
supported
The TSP tree detects temporal coherence independently of spatial brick size [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the TSP tree 'decouples spatial and temporal domains' to address issues where 'resolution discrepancies prevent detecting temporal coherence in small subvolumes' (which are determined by spatial brick size). It contrasts this with 4D octrees, where temporal coherence for subvolumes smaller than the spatial subdivision size cannot be detected. By decoupling the domains, the TSP tree allows temporal coherence to be detected independently of the spatial brick size constraints.
supported
When rendering a different time step, repeat traversal [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that 'When rendering a different time step, repeat traversal.' It further explains that if nodes with high temporal coherence are encountered and stored intermediate results cover the current time step, the rendering can be skipped and results reused. This directly supports the claim.
supported
It uses a similar hierarchical structure (octree with temporal binary trees) but operates on wavelet coefficients rather than raw voxel values [S3].

The claim states that the method uses a hierarchical structure (octree with temporal binary trees) and operates on wavelet coefficients. The evidence explicitly mentions a 'Time Space Partitioning Tree structure which is made by an octree whose nodes contain a binary tree with temporal information' and notes that a 'similar approach has been applied to a 3D wavelet transformation of the original data using a Wavelet-based TSP.' This confirms both the structural description and the operation on wavelet coefficients.
supported
In 4D octrees, if a subvolume has dramatic spatial variation but remains unchanged temporally, overall value coherence appears low, causing temporal coherence to be missed [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that in 4D octrees, if a subvolume has dramatic spatial variation but remains unchanged temporally, overall value coherence appears low, causing temporal coherence to be missed. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Another problem of using the four-dimensional trees is that coupling spatial and temporal domains makes it difficult to locate regions with only temporal coherence but not spatial coherence... Let us assume that a subvolume has a dramatic value variation within the spatial domain but remains unchanged across several time steps. In four-dimensional space the overall value coherence would appear to be low even though the temporal coherence alone has a strong presence. As a result, the temporal coherence is not detected.' This matches the claim exactly.
